Action Plan:
1. Arrange same-day in-person assessment at the central London clinic for full examination to identify the source of fever.
2. Following examination, proceed with blood tests including thick and thin blood films for malaria and inflammatory markers; additional tests at the examining clinician’s discretion. Urgency of laboratory testing to be determined by findings on exam.
3. If unable to attend the central clinic, attend a local Emergency Department (A&E) and present this note at reception.
4. Do not attend work until the cause of fever is identified and clinical fitness is clarified.
5. Clinician to message admin to book the clinic visit; patient to call the number provided in the consultation notes to confirm a slot today.
6. Verbal consent from patient has been obtained before using transcription software.

Subjective:
- Reason for visit: 7 days of fever with alternating hot/cold episodes, night sweats, diffuse myalgias, nausea with poor oral intake, and fatigue. OTC ibuprofen and acetaminophen provide only partial relief.
- Associated symptoms: Denies cough, sore throat, ear pain, diarrhea, neck stiffness, new/worsening headaches (reports baseline screen-related headaches), rash, joint swelling/tenderness, dysuria, urinary frequency, or urgency.
- Travel history: Returned from Vietnam 4 weeks ago; mix of urban and rural travel with trekking and cycling through farmland; trip described as adventurous. Took malaria prophylaxis but cannot recall the name; believes it was a daily tablet and thinks there was an additional tablet “on top of the first one.”
- Past medical history: Chronic back pain related to prolonged sitting/poor posture; currently under physiotherapy.
- Medications:
  - Seroxat (paroxetine) — dose/route/frequency not documented.
  - Ibuprofen (OTC) — dose/route/frequency not documented; patient reports taking recommended dose daily.
  - Acetaminophen/paracetamol (OTC) — dose/route/frequency not documented; patient reports taking recommended dose daily.
- Allergies: Pollen (hay fever). No medication allergies reported.
- Family history: Father had a myocardial infarction at age 68.
- Social history: Works as a nurse; vaccinations up to date including Hepatitis B. Non-smoker. Moderate alcohol intake. Performs moderate exercise a few times per week.

Objective:
- No vitals recorded.
- No physical examination performed during this telehealth consult.
- No investigation results available at this time.

Assessment & Plan:

1. Acute febrile illness post-travel to Vietnam:
   - Assessment/likely diagnosis: Acute febrile illness without clear localizing source; must rule out malaria.
   - Differential diagnosis: Malaria; chest infection; throat infection; other “exotic infections” related to recent travel (as discussed).
   - Investigations planned: In-person physical examination; blood tests including thick and thin blood films for malaria; inflammatory markers; additional tests per examining clinician. Urgency to be guided by examination findings.
   - Treatment planned: Advise patient to refrain from work until evaluation is complete and fitness clarified.
   - Relevant referrals: Same-day clinic assessment in central London; alternative option to attend local Emergency Department (A&E) if clinic attendance is not feasible.

2. Occupational fitness for work:
   - Assessment/likely diagnosis: Temporarily unfit for work due to ongoing febrile illness pending diagnostic clarification.
   - Treatment planned: Do not attend work until medically cleared after evaluation.

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements: Vital signs (including measured temperature, heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation); full physical exam; pregnancy status/LMP; detailed medication doses/routes/frequencies; specific malaria prophylaxis name/dose/adherence schedule; additional travel exposure details (e.g., freshwater exposure, mosquito bite frequency, food/water hygiene, vaccinations for travel); COVID-19 status/testing; sick contacts; hydration status/urine output trends.
- Internal conflicts: None noted.
- Transcript quality: Generally clear with minor hesitations and brief pauses; adequate for documentation.
